## The preregistration of the replication {#the-preregistration-of-the-replication .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **Registered first.** The plan was uploaded on 5 May 2020 and registered on the OSF on 14 May 2020 (osf.io/v6wd8); the final report followed on 7 October 2020
- **What it fixed.** The four names, the housing authorities on the HUD list, the outcome (any use of the first or the last name), a sample of 738 replies set by a power analysis, and the main analysis: a linear probability model without covariates, on a random draw of 738 replies
- **What the report added.** A logistic regression with census covariates, on the authorities that could be matched with census data, to match Table 1 of the paper; the report lists both changes as deviations from the plan
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Because the plan came first, a reader can tell the analysis that was promised from the one that was added, and judge each of them on that basis.
:::

::: {.src}
osf.io/2ug8x – the preregistration and the final report of the replication; osf.io/v6wd8 – the registration.
:::

::: notes
The replication wrote its plan down and registered it before the first email went out, in May 2020, and the final report followed in October. The plan fixed the four names, the housing authorities to be emailed, the outcome, which was any use of the first or the last name, the size of the sample, which came from a power analysis, and the main analysis: a plain difference in proportions on a random draw of seven hundred and thirty-eight replies. The report repeated that draw a thousand times, and the gap was not significant in about ninety-three per cent of them. [advance] The report also contains analyses that the plan did not promise: a logistic regression with census covariates, on the authorities that could be matched with census data, added so that the result could be set beside Table 1 of the paper. The report lists both changes as deviations from the plan. Because the plan came first, you can tell which analysis was promised and which was added, and weigh them accordingly.
:::

## What a preregistration fixes {#what-a-preregistration-fixes .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**Fixed before any result exists**

- The claim that is tested, and the question behind it
- The data, and what you already know about them
- One option for each decision of the analysis
- The reason for those choices
- What will count as support, and what will not
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**Left open**

- Whether the choices were good ones
- Whether the specification estimates the quantity that the question implies
- Whether its assumptions hold
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
A preregistration protects a choice from its result. The estimand statement of this morning is what justifies the choice.
:::

::: notes
So what does a preregistration fix? On the left, five things, which are also the fields of the block that you are about to fill in. The claim and the question behind it, which you wrote this morning as an estimand statement. The data, and, for data that already exist, what you know about them before you choose. One option for each decision of the analysis. The reason for those choices. And the rule, written before any result, for what will count as support. On the right, what it leaves open: whether the choices were good ones, whether they estimate the quantity that the question implies, and whether the assumptions hold. A badly reasoned plan that is registered is still badly reasoned. [advance] That is why the estimand came first today. The preregistration protects the choice from its result, and the reasoning about the question is what makes the choice worth protecting.
:::
